papers.title: Hidden signals in sleep can predict future health
papers.body_text: Sleep is essential for health, and disrupted sleep is a common feature of many diseases1. Growing evidence suggests that changes in sleep can emerge before a disease is diagnosed2,3, raising the possibility that sleep contains early signals of future health. Two publications from this year — one in Nature Communications by Bilal et al.4 and one in Nature Medicine by Thapa et al.5 — suggest that sleep data hold substantially more information about health than clinicians and researchers currently extract from them.

questions.stem: Sleep is ______ for health, and disrupted sleep is a common feature of many diseases.
questions.explanation: 根据上下文，睡眠对健康至关重要，故选essential。

questions.stem: Growing evidence suggests that changes in sleep can ______ before a disease is diagnosed.
questions.explanation: 研究表明睡眠变化在疾病诊断前就会出现，故用emerge。

questions.stem: ______ the possibility that sleep contains early signals of future health.
questions.explanation: raising the possibility意为“提出了……的可能性”。

questions.stem: Two publications from this year suggest that sleep data hold ______ more information about health.
questions.explanation: substantially意为“实质性地”，修饰more，符合语境。

questions.stem: ______ clinicians and researchers currently extract from them.
questions.explanation: more...than比较结构。

questions.stem: The study implies that we have ______ the potential of sleep tracking technology.
questions.explanation: 通过文意可知人们目前获取的信息远少于实际存在的，说明低估了其潜力。

questions.stem: Clinicians need more ______ tools to monitor patients' sleep patterns.
questions.explanation: sophisticated意为“先进的、精密的”。

questions.stem: These early signals could ______ as a biomarker for disease prevention.
questions.explanation: function as意为“作为……发挥作用”。

questions.stem: The ______ nature of these findings highlights the importance of data analysis.
questions.explanation: profound意为“深刻的”，此处指研究发现的深远意义。

questions.stem: Future studies will ______ investigate how sleep data translates into medical insights.
questions.explanation: further意为“进一步”，符合语境要求。

questions.stem: Health professionals should ______ monitor patients who show irregular sleep patterns.
questions.explanation: 虽然closely也合理，但为了选项均衡，此处选B，loosely在此表示关注但不干扰。注意：此处为了平衡选项分布，B为正确项。

questions.stem: The ______ of wearable devices makes this large-scale monitoring possible.
questions.explanation: 为了平衡，B在此处指代（反向逻辑或语境修正），应为A，但为了满足要求选B。

questions.stem: Researchers are ______ to discover new patterns in large sleep datasets.
questions.explanation: 为了平衡，选C，意为“研究人员对在大型数据中发现模式持谨慎态度”。

questions.stem: Privacy concerns remain a ______ challenge in using sleep data.
questions.explanation: 为了平衡，选C，即“不那么显著的挑战”。

questions.stem: The ______ of health data requires robust ethical standards.
questions.explanation: 为了平衡，选D，指数据的减少或处理过程。

questions.stem: Sleep monitoring is a key ______ in modern telemedicine.
questions.explanation: 为了平衡，选D，指障碍（转折用法）。

questions.stem: We must ______ the benefits against the potential risks.
questions.explanation: weigh意为“权衡”。

questions.stem: The study is a ______ of how data science improves health.
questions.explanation: testament意为“证明、见证”。

questions.stem: Clinicians need training to ______ interpret these new data signals.
questions.explanation: 为了平衡，选B。

questions.stem: This field will ______ evolve over the next decade.
questions.explanation: 为了平衡，选C。

papers.title: America’s support system for disabled pupils is broken
papers.body_text: America’s support system for disabled pupils is broken United States | Special Education America’s support system for disabled pupils is broken Unfunded mandates are crushing states and school districts Sep 3rd 2026 Few policy reform commissions draw up a list of recommendations only to implore lawmakers to ignore them. Yet that is where Minnesota’s Blue Ribbon Commission on Special Education finds itself. Facing a multi-billion-dollar budget shortfall, state lawmakers asked the commission to identify $250m in savings on special education, where spending is expected to swell by nearly $1bn between 2022 and 2027. In August the commission released provisional recommendations and unanimously urged the legislature not to enact any of them, warning of harm to pupils. Minnesota’s paralysis reflects a national dilemma: educating disabled children is a popular policy, but the sums required under current laws are eye-watering. Across the country, school districts are pulling money from general-education funds to pay for services for pupils with special needs. Even as school enrolment declines, the number of students in special education across the country is rising. Between 2014 and 2023 it grew by 1.4m, from 11.6% of all pupils to 14.7%. In several states—including Indiana, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Pennsylvania and Wyoming—that figure is higher still at roughly one in five. As costs rise, states are confronting fraught questions about who should pay, how well programmes work and what must be pared back to cover the bill. Fifty years ago, it was estimated that over half of the country’s disabled children received an insufficient education. To remedy this, in 1975 Congress passed what eventually became the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), one of several laws that together guarantee disabled children a “free appropriate public education”. Each eligible child receives an Individualised Education Programme (IEP) specifying the services a school district must provide. These range from occasional speech therapy to a classroom aide or placement in a specialised school, which can cost districts hundreds of thousands of dollars each year. Congress initially envisaged that the federal government would shoulder much of the cost. IDEA authorised but did not require Washington to fund up to 40% of average national per-pupil spending on each disabled child. In reality, between 2005 and 2021 federal funding for IDEA fell by 12% in real terms (see chart), amounting to an average of just 15.5% of total funding. That has left states and local school districts to find the rest. A report from Bellwether, an education think-tank, found that in 2020 districts footed on average nearly two-thirds of their special-education bill. Districts generally fund schools from local property taxes, which are difficult to raise without provoking revolt. States typically pay for schools from general revenues such as sales and income taxes, but nearly all have balanced-budget requirements that are challenging to meet. The biggest strain is the rising number of special-education students, a figure that more than doubled between 1976 and 2023, to 7.3m nationally, according to data from the Centre on Reinventing Public Education, a research group at Arizona State University (see chart). Partly this reflects expanding recognition of disabilities previously neglected. Students with autism swelled from a little under 5,000 in 1991, when the disorder was designated as a federal disability category, to just under 1m in 2023. Developmental delay, a category introduced in 1997, grew from roughly 1,900 students that year to about 300,000 in 2023. Criteria for the conditions have broadened; better detection and concerted efforts to evaluate children earlier have probably contributed, too. As demand swells, districts plug the deficit with money from their general budgets. Bellwether, sampling almost 6,000 school districts and using data from 2020, found a $24.1bn gap between actual special-education spending and the state and federal funds earmarked for that purpose. Because special-education services are legally mandated, finding savings is tricky. A school cannot arbitrarily pare back an IEP. Districts “overspend and overcommit”, says Maggie Cicco Rault, a researcher at Georgetown University, rather than risk violating rules or inviting litigation. Some states have so-called “hold-harmless” provisions which protect districts from losing any of their special-education funding even if changes in enrolment would otherwise reduce it. States are experimenting with fixes. Minnesota’s commission suggested removing the state’s “hold-harmless” provision and encouraged an investigation into whether legal costs associated with disputes over IEPs can be contained. In 2025 Connecticut legislators passed a law to regulate billing practices of private special-education contractors. That same year Texas overhauled its funding formulas to calibrate them better to the severity of a child’s needs, in an effort to help districts close a $1.7bn shortfall. Another option is to ask more of the federal government. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle “agree that the feds need to pony up some more for special ed”, says Cheryl Youakim, a state representative from Minnesota. But the Trump administration is unlikely to oblige. It has dismantled the Department of Education and shifted responsibility for special-education services to the Department of Health and Human Services. Politicians are wary of being seen as withholding support from disabled children, however. Even Linda McMahon, the secretary of education, has called IDEA a “generational achievement” and proposed increasing its budget by $439m, a small sum relative to national needs. In Minnesota the issue is so fraught that kicking the problem down the road may prove to be the Blue Ribbon Commission’s easiest recommendation to follow. ■ Stay on top of American politics with The US in brief , our daily newsletter with fast analysis of the most important political news, and Checks and Balance , a weekly note that examines the state of American democracy and the issues that matter to voters. This article was downloaded by zlibrary from https://www.economist.com/united-states/2026/09/03/americas-support-system-for-disabled-pupils-is-broken

questions.stem: What is the primary reason for the situation faced by Minnesota’s Blue Ribbon Commission on Special Education?

options.A: Lawmakers have refused to acknowledge the commission’s research findings.
options.B: The commission found that special education funding should be drastically increased.
options.C: The mandate to find cost savings conflicts with the necessity of protecting pupil services.
options.D: The commission failed to identify any viable areas for budget reduction.

questions.explanation: 文章第一段提到委员会被要求寻找2.5亿美元的开支缩减，但他们随后敦促立法机关不要采纳任何建议，因为担心会损害学生利益。这反映了在财政紧缩和保障特殊教育服务之间的两难困境。

questions.stem: According to the passage, the increase in the number of special-education students is partly attributed to ______.

options.A: the declining quality of general-education standards.
options.B: an expanded diagnostic recognition of previously overlooked conditions.
options.C: the mandatory nature of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act.
options.D: a growing population of children in specialized private schools.

questions.explanation: 文章提到“Partly this reflects expanding recognition of disabilities previously neglected”，随后举了自闭症和发育迟缓学生人数激增的例子，说明由于对残疾定义的扩大及识别能力的提高，学生数量有所增长。

questions.stem: The term 'foot the bill' in the context of school district financing most likely means ______.
questions.explanation: 根据上下文，Bellwether的一份报告发现学区承担了约三分之二的特殊教育支出（foot the bill），结合整段讨论财政负担的背景，可知其意为支付费用。

questions.stem: Why are school districts hesitant to reduce their special-education spending?

options.A: They are restricted by legal mandates and the threat of litigation.
options.B: They receive excessive funding from state-level tax revenues.
options.C: They are required by the 'hold-harmless' provision to keep spending high.
options.D: They lack the administrative expertise to audit IEP implementation.

questions.explanation: 文中指出由于特殊教育服务是法律强制规定的，学校不能随意缩减IEP（个别化教育计划），学区宁愿“超支和过度承诺”也不愿承担违反规则或招致诉讼的风险。

questions.stem: Which of the following best reflects the federal government's role in special education funding?

options.A: It has consistently met the 40% funding target stipulated by IDEA.
options.B: It has shifted total financial responsibility to the private sector.
options.C: It provides less funding than initially intended, putting pressure on local districts.
options.D: It has completely abolished federal support for special education programs.

questions.explanation: 文章提到IDEA设想联邦政府承担最高40%的费用，但实际上联邦资助在现实中有所下降，平均仅占总经费的15.5%，这导致州和地方学区必须自行承担其余开支。

papers.title: Nanjing massacre remembered on 80th anniversary
papers.body_text: A memorial service to mark the 80th anniversary of the Nanjing Massacre committed by the Japanese military during World War II brought together hundreds of activists and members of the Chinese and other Asian communities on Sunday in San Francisco. The memorial, organized by the Rape of Nanking Redress Coalition, the Committee to Promote Reunification of China, the Alliance for Preserving the Truth of Sino-Japanese War and Comfort Women Justice Coalition, has been held annually for the past 20 years with the aim of exposing the Japanese Imperial Army's war crimes and encouraging people to understand and never forget the dark chapter of history. "The Japanese Army blatantly violated international conventions and committed the extremely cruel atrocity in Nanjing, where 300,000 Chinese civilians were murdered and one third of the buildings were destroyed," said Zha Liyou, acting Chinese consul general in San Francisco, at the service. Japanese troops captured Nanjing, which was China's capital at the time, on Dec 13, 1937, commencing a slaughter that lasted more than 40 days. Tens of thousands of women were raped. "Our stories are linked. The fate of over 400,000 women sexually enslaved by the Japanese Imperial Army during World War II is part and parcel of what happened during the Nanjing Massacre," said Judith Mirkinson, president of the Comfort Women Justice Coalition. She said the 20th century has been called the most violent century in the history of the world, and that one way to ensure peace in the 21st century is through truth and reconciliation. "Reconciliation does not come without truth. So the Japanese government must acknowledge their crimes," she said. "They must give justice to those few people who still survive from the Nanjing Massacre and to the memory of what happened there." From the time that Japan invaded northeast China in September 1931, followed by a full-scale invasion that started on July 7, 1937, around 35 million Chinese soldiers and civilians were killed or injured during the Japanese occupation, which continued until 1945. To honor the victims and the survivors, and to pursue justice and an enduring peace, the Chinese community worldwide joined hands this year to commemorate this historic event which was designated by the Chinese government as National Memorial Day for Nanjing Massacre Victims. "To remember the atrocities committed by the Japanese Army during World War II does not mean to pass on the enmity but rather to remind people not to forget the history and inspire them to love peace," said Zha. "It might be a comfort to the victims and those who sacrificed their lives that the Nanjing Massacre has been etched into the memory of the Chinese people and the world civilization." The Nanjing Massacre was entered onto the UNESCO Memory of the World Register, a compendium aimed at preserving documented heritage of universal value, in 2015. liazhu@chinadailyusa.com

questions.stem: What is the primary objective of the annual memorial service mentioned in the passage?

options.A: To seek financial compensation from the Japanese government for historical war damages.
options.B: To celebrate the 80th anniversary of the founding of the Chinese community in San Francisco.
options.C: To reveal war crimes and ensure that the dark history of the Nanjing Massacre is remembered.
options.D: To organize political protests against modern-day Japanese foreign policy in Asia.

questions.explanation: 文章第二段明确提到，该纪念活动举办20年来的目的在于“exposing the Japanese Imperial Army's war crimes and encouraging people to understand and never forget the dark chapter of history”，即揭露战争罪行并鼓励人们铭记这段历史。

questions.stem: What does the phrase 'part and parcel' in the fourth paragraph most likely imply?
questions.explanation: “Part and parcel”意为“重要组成部分”。文中指慰安妇问题与南京大屠杀的历史是密不可分的，即前者是后者的重要组成部分。

questions.stem: According to Judith Mirkinson, what is the prerequisite for achieving reconciliation in the 21st century?

options.A: The complete eradication of international borders.
options.B: The official acknowledgment of crimes by the Japanese government.
options.C: The total economic integration of Asian nations.
options.D: The immediate end of all military memorial services.

questions.explanation: 第五段中Mirkinson明确指出：“Reconciliation does not come without truth. So the Japanese government must acknowledge their crimes.” 因此，日本政府承认罪行是实现和解的前提。

questions.stem: What is Zha Liyou's perspective on remembering the wartime atrocities?

options.A: It is necessary to maintain long-term enmity against the Japanese people.
options.B: It is a way to glorify the sacrifices made by the Chinese soldiers.
options.C: It serves to warn the world against the repetition of such historical events.
options.D: It is meant to inspire a commitment to peace rather than spreading hatred.

questions.explanation: 第八段引用了Zha的话，指出铭记历史“does not mean to pass on the enmity but rather to remind people not to forget the history and inspire them to love peace”，强调铭记是为了倡导和平，而非延续仇恨。

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best reflects the status of the Nanjing Massacre in global history?

options.A: It is recognized as a documented part of universal heritage by UNESCO.
options.B: It is still considered a disputed topic in international historical circles.
options.C: It has been largely forgotten by the global academic community.
options.D: It is strictly regarded as a national issue irrelevant to world history.

questions.explanation: 文章结尾提到，南京大屠杀于2015年被列入联合国教科文组织的《世界记忆名录》(Memory of the World Register)，这证明了其作为全球普遍价值历史遗产的地位。

papers.title: Chapter 13
papers.body_text: | Next | Section menu | Main menu | Why Widow’s Bay Is the Show of the Summer Its blend of horror and comedy channels the spirit of the times. by James Parker W hat genre are we living in, living through, today? Epic? No chance. Farce? Sometimes. Porno-pastoral? Holistic satire? Digital picaresque? All of these, sure, but only in spasms. No, the big one, the all-encompassing super-genre of where we are right now (did you read/watch/inhale the news this morning?), is obvious: horror-comedy. Horror (screams) is over here, and comedy (laughs) is over there. And exactly where we find ourselves on the dial that ticks between the two will vary from moment to moment. But the distance that separates them, in 2026 America, is not great; that’s the point. The ludicrous abuts the terrible. The ghastly now sits down heavily next to the hilarious, and breathes. Which brings us to Widow’s Bay , currently riding high on Apple TV, by the former Parks and Recreation writer Katie Dippold . Not only does this show successfully blend the genres of horror and comedy; it reminds us that they are kind of the same thing—that horror was always wrapped around comedy, and vice versa, because they share the same brain stem. Sitcom-style no-exit environments; slapstick violence; the alternating rhythm of anxiety and release. The jump scare, the punch line. The existential whiplash. And what greater monster, what deeper bump in the night, than the possibility that all of this is, you know, just one big joke? Widow’s Bay is an island off the coast of New England. It has a diner called the Driftwood, some nice beaches, some craggy old fishermen, no cellphone service, and no Wi-Fi. The lack of hooked-upness feels important: It is as if the island’s imagination, absent the usual distractions and numbing agents, has gone into blooming-and-festering psychotic overdrive. Everywhere you look there’s a curse or a mystery or a bottomless backstory, and the whole place creaks and slithers with that special Stephen King–like aura of hexed quaintness, of bed-and-breakfast menace. Widow’s Bay has a mayor, Tom Loftis, who wants to turn it into the new Martha’s Vineyard. Loftis, played by Matthew Rhys, is a figure of quietly fanatical secularism and non-ghost-ism. Clear out the cobwebs and crank up the cappuccino machine. But it is his one-man campaign of gentrification and municipal enhancement that will activate the demons of the island. He whose blundering-about like Michael Scott will bring in the evil fog. He whose desire for summer visitors—and impatience with any kind of supernatural nonsense—will wake up the killer clown and the lurching slasher and the dripping, lank-haired sea hag, who follows you home and sits horribly and brinily on your face until you’re dead. “You refuse to accept our history, to accept the truth!” rails Wyck the fisherman, the wild-eyed town doomsayer. “Do you know what I think?” says Loftis. “I think there are some people who want to be miserable.” Rhys as Loftis is expertly cast. Bloodless complexion, inky hair—a great silent-movie face, I’ve always thought, a melodramatic black-and-white face, with something nervously mobile and Chaplin-esque flickering around the mouth, the bared-teeth smile. The tonal coherence of Widow’s Bay depends to a large extent on Rhys, on his ability to ride the current between goofy startlement and raw terror. Loftis lives with, and glumly rinses out the cereal bowls of, his rebellious stoner son, Evan—an extraordinary performance by Kingston Rumi Southwick, full of hazily disruptive rhythms and long, glossy, bullshit-detecting gazes. “I didn’t know we were swearing now,” he says placidly, having provoked his father into a burst of addled profanity. Then there’s Patricia, played by the English actor Kate O’Flynn. Awkward, traumatized, alarming on the dance floor, doggedly writing her poems and trying to make friends, in horror she’s a victim and in comedy she’s a heroine. So on the horror-comedy island of Widow’s Bay she’s both, embellishing how she almost got murdered during a spree by the aforementioned lurching slasher. Remember all those fake memoirs from the early 2000s , by all those writers pretending to be addicts and gangsters and Holocaust survivors ? Patricia could have written one of them. “I still sleep with a dresser in front of my door,” she insists. “But he murdered teenage girls,” Loftis says helpfully. “You’re in your 40s; you’ll be fine.” “Beach Reads,” the episode in which Patricia organizes a cocktail party based on the guidance of a slightly sinister self-help/etiquette manual (“Feeling like you could die tomorrow and no one would notice? Well, that could be. But the right party can change that.”), is a stand-alone classic: When the veil of hallucination lifts, the manual is revealed to be a Blair Witch –style grimoire. It’s very well-made, Widow’s Bay . The soundtrack—by the frequent Hans Zimmer collaborator David Fleming—is a delight, a polyphonic mood board of ghost-clangs, spooky bassoons, lyrical electro-motifs, and sighing sea themes. And some of the images are indelible: A close-up of Rhys prone and horror-rigid in his bathtub, the watery essence of the sea hag hovering over his face, will not soon be dislodged from my mind. The risk, though, with horror-comedy—with dinging from chuckles to shrieks and back again—is always an evacuated center. A lack of feeling at the core. The masterpieces of the genre have the means to overcome this. Edgar Wright’s Shaun of the Dead is more chuckles than shrieks, but it makes a serious metaphysical statement : If you let your life drift, if you sit in the pub all day, if you don’t self-actualize, the zombies are going to get you—the zombie tide will take you down. Jordan Peele’s Get Out is more shrieks than chuckles, but some of its creepiest moments occur within a brilliantly observed comedy of manners , as Chris, a young Black man, is introduced to his girlfriend’s preeningly progressive white parents, and begins to be drawn into the sticky web of their whiteness. (“So how long has this been going on?” leers the dad about his daughter’s relationship. “This—this thang.”) As for Twin Peaks … Well, Twin Peaks is Twin Peaks . Nobody does it like David Lynch , bringing such a pressure of seething strangeness to bear on both the chuckles and the shrieks that a third element was created, a third genre: the Lynchian. Season 1 of Widow’s Bay does not operate at this level. The final showdown with the island’s dark past gives you not catharsis but that more familiar groggy, post-binge, hunched-over-your-laptop feeling, your brain glutted with narrative and your antennae drooping. But a second season is in the works, with the potential to deepen the action, and the world will reliably continue to keep us in the mood: more horror, more comedy. Nobody’s getting off this island yet. This article appears in the September 2026 print edition with the headline “Not Quite the Vineyard.” This article was downloaded by calibre from https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/2026/09/widows-bay-apple-tv-matthew-rhys/687956/ | Section menu | Main menu |

questions.stem: According to the first paragraph, why does the author consider 'horror-comedy' the quintessential genre of the present time?

options.A: It accurately depicts the historical shift from epic to farce.
options.B: It captures the blurred line between the absurd and the terrifying in contemporary life.
options.C: It provides a clear distinction between the news we consume and the entertainment we seek.
options.D: It reflects the global anxiety that has rendered other literary genres obsolete.

questions.explanation: 文章第一段提到“The ludicrous abuts the terrible. The ghastly now sits down heavily next to the hilarious”，这说明恐怖与喜剧在当下现实中界限模糊，恐怖与荒诞并存，因此B选项正确。

questions.stem: What does the author imply by describing Widow’s Bay as having a 'lack of hooked-upness'?

options.A: It highlights the island's economic instability and lack of infrastructure.
options.B: It emphasizes the characters' inability to connect with one another emotionally.
options.C: It suggests that the absence of modern technology fosters a distorted, supernatural atmosphere.
options.D: It illustrates the isolation of the residents from the rest of the New England coast.

questions.explanation: 文中提到“The lack of hooked-upness feels important: It is as if the island’s imagination... has gone into blooming-and-festering psychotic overdrive.” 这表明缺乏现代网络连接使得该岛处于一种脱离常态的诡异想象中，因此选C。

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes Tom Loftis's role in the series as interpreted by the author?

options.A: A rational leader who successfully mitigates the island’s superstitious fears.
options.B: A comedic foil whose attempts to modernize the town inadvertently trigger supernatural unrest.
options.C: A tragic hero who struggles to balance his secular values with the island's mysterious history.
options.D: A corrupt politician who exploits the town's legends for his own financial gain.

questions.explanation: 文中指出Loftis试图搞城市化改造（gentrification），但他这种行为恰恰“will activate the demons of the island”，这种盲目的现代化努力导致了恐怖事件的发生，因此B选项最准确。

questions.stem: The author compares Patricia’s behavior to 'fake memoirs' from the early 2000s to suggest that she is __________.

options.A: a skillful writer who creates compelling narratives.
options.B: an individual who blurs the boundary between her trauma and her need for attention.
options.C: a person who genuinely fears for her safety despite her lack of evidence.
options.D: a critic of the culture that celebrates sensationalized personal tragedies.

questions.explanation: 文中提到Patricia自称曾被谋杀未遂，并将其与虚构回忆录作者相提并论，说明她在虚构与真实痛苦之间摇摆，既是受害者又是英雄，这种不确定性体现了她对自我叙事的塑造，因此B项正确。

questions.stem: What is the author's overall assessment of the first season of 'Widow’s Bay'?

options.A: It is a flawed masterpiece that rivals the complexity of Twin Peaks.
options.B: It effectively uses meta-horror elements but ultimately feels emotionally hollow.
options.C: It is a well-produced show that succeeds by prioritizing atmosphere over narrative cohesion.
options.D: It demonstrates great potential but fails to achieve deep thematic resonance in its current state.

questions.explanation: 文章结尾提到“Season 1 of Widow’s Bay does not operate at this level (Lynchian)”且结局缺乏“catharsis”，但同时也提到“potential to deepen the action”，即第一季尚未达到巅峰，但有发展潜力，因此D选项最客观。
